title: HPA Axis Stress Dial
description: Interactive model of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Learners set stress intensity and choose a single acute stressor or daily chronic stress, then watch CRH, ACTH, and cortisol rise and fall on a graph. A negative-feedback switch shows how cortisol turns the system off. A gut panel shows colon movement, gut sensitivity, and gut permeability responding to stress signaling.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Explain the order of the HPA axis cascade: CRH from the hypothalamus, ACTH from the pituitary, and cortisol from the adrenal cortex.
Explain how cortisol's negative feedback returns the HPA axis to baseline after acute stress, and why repeated chronic stress keeps reactivating it.
Describe how stress signaling changes the gut: faster colon movement and, with repeated stress, more sensitivity and permeability.
prerequisites: Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood
The autonomic nervous system and gut motility (Chapter 1)
keyQuestions: Which hormone rises first after a stressor, and which rises last?
What does cortisol do to CRH and ACTH, and why does that matter?
How does the pattern change when stress happens every day?
Why can stress speed up the colon even though fight-or-flight slows digestion?
misconceptions: Cortisol is purely harmful and should always be as low as possible.
The adrenal glands stop making cortisol because they run out, rather than because of negative feedback.
Acute stress and chronic stress affect the body in the same way.
